body.p: Use this feature to generate a report that contains a content-aware fingerprint (hash) for every file in a directory or archive. Unlike a plain checksum of a file's bytes, this fingerprint reflects the file's meaningful content. The same "ignore" settings available in the Compare Directories tool (ignore attribute order, ignore whitespaces, ignore specific nodes by XPath, etc.) can be applied before the hash is computed. Therefore, two files that differ only in ways you choose to disregard produce the same hash.

This is especially useful when you need to check whether the same content is deployed identically across multiple locations (servers, branches, or environments) without running pairwise comparisons between every pair of locations. Generate a report for each location, then compare the hash values for matching file paths. No direct access between the locations is required.

section.title: Generating a Report

fig.title: Generate Hash Report for Directory Dialog Box

section.p:
To generate a hash report:
Go to Tools Comparison Tools Generate Hash Report for Directory .
In the Directory or archive field, browse to or enter the path to the directory or archive to fingerprint.
In the Report file field, choose where to save the generated XML report.
If the Open in Editor option is selected, the report will be opened in the editor once generated.
(Optional) In the Diff options configuration file field, select a JSON, YAML, or XML configuration file that specifies the differences to ignore when computing hashes. This is the same format used by the scripting comparison arguments. If you leave this field empty, no differences are ignored, and hashes reflect the exact file content.
Click Generate report.

p.note: If you plan to compare hash values across reports generated separately (for example, for different locations and possibly by different people), ensure that every report uses the same diff options configuration file. Hashes computed with different ignore settings cannot be compared, even when the content is identical.

section.title: Content Type Coverage

row.entry: XML, XHTML, HTML, XSL, XSD, RNG, Schematron, XProc, WSDL, SVG, DITA maps
Canonical form of the parsed document tree
All: ignore attribute order, ignore whitespaces, ignore nodes by XPath, ignore expansion state of empty elements, etc.
Markdown, CSS, LESS, JavaScript, JSON, JSON5, JSONL, YAML, and other formats with syntax highlighting support
Canonical form of the tokenized content
Plain text or unrecognized content, or content that fails to parse
Raw byte fingerprint of the file

section.p: When a file falls back to a raw byte fingerprint, the report flags it with an additionalInfo attribute explaining why (unsupported content type, or a parsing failure).

section.title: Report Format
section.codeblock: <fileHashReport directoryPath="D:/deployments/location-046" diffOptionsFilePath="D:/deployments/diffOptions.json"> <meta name="description" content="File hash report"/> <meta name="author" content="Oxygen XML App Suite"/> <meta name="userName" content="john_doe"/> <meta name="reportTimestamp" content="2026-09-17T10:18:01.3927923"/> <meta name="diffOptions" content= " Include files filter:*; Include folders filter:*; Exclude files filter:.DS_Store; Exclude folders filter:CVS,.svn,_svn,.git; ...... Ignore prefixes:false; Ignore attribute order:true; Ignore expansion state for empty elements:true;"/> <dir name="app"> <file name="log.xml" path="app/log.xml" size="1204" modified="2026-09-16T11:30:12.374Z" hash="7e83f485e6ea30e7c7b52614e2f08daaf5c0a6496d5b31091d8a3e162918387f"/> <file name="log-ext.xml" path="app/log-ext.xml" size="2555" modified="2026-09-16T11:31:09.875Z" hash="89dfb8c5f66beabb045d7d6cfd45883fc3593015440baa0054fab7e09730edf9"/> <file name="notes.txt" path="app/notes.txt" size="598" modified="2026-09-16T15:02:10.657Z" hash="1505a90671f30a6c6af075493d77a1b1eb04985ae82716102c42fd8d7c334a64" additionalInfo="hash based on raw file bytes"/> </dir> ...... <file name="results-023.json" path="results-023.json" size="4522" modified="2026-08-16T16:22:19.571Z" hash="1c23bebcbf488bbfa3b6f5f2be6c82a1d490b7a641eda526570ee9ffd0233b4c"/> </fileHashReport>
section.p: File paths are relative to the directory for which the hash report was generated. Therefore, the same file at the same relative location in different reports can be matched directly (for example, through a SQL join on path), even when the reports are generated independently on different machines and from different absolute locations.

ul.li: For JSON and YAML content, property order is significant. Two files that are otherwise identical but have properties in a different order produce different hashes, although property order has no meaning in JSON or YAML itself.

For HTML content, attribute order is generally preserved, and the ignore attribute order option works as expected. However, if a file is sufficiently "malformed" to require the most lenient internal HTML-to-XHTML conversion step, that step alphabetically normalizes attributes, and the option has no effect for that file.

section.title: Example: Verifying Consistent Deployment Across Multiple Locations
section.p: If you manage the same content deployed across many separate locations (servers, branches, or environments), you can use the generated reports to detect drift without directly comparing every pair of locations. Generate a report for each location, using the same diff options configuration file for all reports (see the important note above), and then compare the reports.

The most actionable approach is to designate one location's report as the reference (a known-good or golden copy, a certified build, a production baseline, etc.) and compare every other location's report with it. Comparing reports with a reference immediately identifies which locations deviated and how. This information is needed for further investigation, so use this approach first when you have a location, build, or environment that you trust to be correct.
This example assumes that the reports are collected in one folder and queried as a collection, and that the reference report's file name is known in advance:

The reference report's path/hash pairs are loaded once into a map ($referenceHashes), then every <file> in every report in the collection (including the reference report itself, which trivially matches its own hashes and so never appears in the result) is checked against it. The result lists every file, in every location, whose hash does not match the reference (exactly the locations and files worth investigating further). The user attribute (from the report's own <meta name="userName">) identifies who generated that report. This is useful when different people run the report for different locations, though if the same person generates several reports for several locations, it will not tell those apart. In that case, report (the report file's own path) is the reliable way to identify the location.

In , the most convenient way to run this query is to define a Collection input that points to the report folder in an XQuery scenario, then use collection() without an argument to refer to it. Alternatively, enable the XPath/XQuery Builder view and run the XQuery code directly in the view.

If you do not yet have a specific reference location to compare with, you can check whether any file differs at all between locations without designating one as the reference. For example, use this as an inexpensive initial check across peer locations that should all be identical, where no location is considered "more correct" than the others:
section.codeblock: for $file in collection('file:///path/to/reports/')//file group by $path := string($file/@path) where count(distinct-values($file/@hash)) > 1 return $path
section.p: This query indicates only that a path has more than one distinct hash across locations, not which location or locations deviated, or from what. Use it as a trigger for further investigation, preferably by choosing one flagged location as a reference and running the preceding comparison, not as a complete diagnosis.
